questions.learningObjective: Trace a tuplet span to find the length of each note.

0.667, meaning each note lasts two thirds of a single eighth note.

options.misconception: Multiplies the tuplet count by the value it replaces.

options.text: 1, meaning each note lasts exactly one eighth note.
options.misconception: Assumes the tuplet leaves the written value alone.

questions.explanation: A duplet is two notes in the time of three, so each note lasts one and a half eighth notes. The figure 2 is a ratio numerator, not a doubling instruction, and the bar keeps its original length.

questions.learningObjective: Name the device that regroups a compound bar into three duple beats.
questions.stem: Bug report BR-118 describes a bar where six eighth notes are felt as three long beats rather than two groups of three, and asks what that device is called.

options.text: A hemiola, which regroups six eighth notes into three even beats of equal weight.
A triplet, which fits three notes into the space normally taken by two.
options.misconception: Confuses a crossed grouping with a simple three against two.

options.text: A syncopation, which shifts the accent away from the strong part of the bar.
options.misconception: Reads the accent shift as an ordinary syncopation.

options.text: A cadenza, which lets a soloist stretch a phrase without accompaniment.
options.misconception: Thinks any free passage of metre is a cadenza.

questions.explanation: A hemiola crosses the metre by regrouping six eighth notes as three beats of two rather than two beats of three. The sounding notes do not change, only the way the bar is felt.
questions.hint: Look for a three-against-two regrouping inside six eighths.

questions.learningObjective: Decide which traced measure is polyphonic from the number of independent lines.
questions.stem: Support request SR-33 traces voice count across four bars: bar 1 has one line, bar 2 has three independent melodies, bar 3 has a melody with chordal support, bar 4 doubles a melody in octaves. Which bar is polyphonic?

options.text: Bar 2, because three separate melodic lines move with real independence.
Bar 3, because the chordal accompaniment adds a second sounding layer.
options.misconception: Counts any extra sounding part as independent polyphony.

options.text: Bar 4, because doubling in octaves creates two moving voices.
options.misconception: Treats octave doubling of one line as two independent parts.

options.text: Bar 1, because a single unaccompanied line is the purest texture.
options.misconception: Believes monophony is a kind of polyphony with fewer voices.

questions.explanation: Polyphony requires melodies that are independent of one another, which only bar 2 provides. Chordal support in bar 3 and octave doubling in bar 4 both stay tied to the tune, so they remain homophonic.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how fugal, two-part and melody-with-accompaniment textures differ.
questions.stem: Story point SP-77 asks the team to explain in their own words how a fugal texture differs from a two-part texture and from a plain melody with accompaniment.

answer.exemplar: A fugal texture is built from several independent voices, each entering with the subject and then its answer, so no single line is simply accompaniment. A two-part texture is also polyphonic, but it divides the music into only two lines and does not require imitation between them. A melody with accompaniment is homophonic: one line carries the tune while the others merely support it and would sound incomplete on their own.

questions.explanation: A fugal texture layers voices that each carry the subject and its answer, while a two-part texture only divides the music into two lines. A melody with accompaniment keeps one line in charge.
questions.hint: Ask which voice is carrying the subject in each case.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a hemiola can make a compound bar sound like simple metre.
questions.stem: Review note RN-44 asks the team to explain why a hemiola in 6/8 can make the bar sound like 3/4 to a listener who follows the accents.

answer.exemplar: In 6/8 the six eighth notes are normally grouped two plus two plus two as two dotted-crotchet beats. A hemiola regroups them three plus three, giving three even crotchet-length beats inside the same bar. Because the music now emphasises three beats where the metre supplies two, a listener who follows the hemiola's accents can hear the bar as 3/4, or even as three half notes stretching the pulse.

questions.explanation: A hemiola borrows a duple accent pattern inside a compound bar, so three groups of two eighths compete with the meter's two groups of three. A listener who follows the new accents hears three beats.
questions.hint: Think of two accents replacing the metrical three.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what distinguishes a sequence from a plain repetition.
questions.stem: Backlog item BK-25 asks what makes a passage a sequence rather than a motive that has simply been repeated.

options.text: The motive is restated at a different pitch level, so the pattern is transposed.
The motive is restated at exactly the same pitch, so it is a new idea.
options.misconception: Considers exact repetition to be a transposing sequence.

options.text: The motive is restated in a different metre, so the pattern is varied.

options.misconception: Treats a change of volume as the defining feature.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the return of the opening section makes a ternary movement feel finished.
questions.stem: Refactor card RC-14 asks the team to explain why the return of the opening section is what makes a ternary movement feel finished.

answer.exemplar: Ternary form feels finished because the middle section is a departure from material the listener already knows, and the return of that opening material closes the circle and answers expectations set at the start. A movement that simply moves from one section to a contrasting one and stops leaves the earlier material unresolved. The repeat of the A section is therefore what turns a pair of contrasted sections into a balanced three-part whole.

questions.explanation: The return of the first section after the contrasting middle gives the movement a closed shape, because the listener hears the material it set out with. Without that return the form stays open and only two-part.
questions.hint: Think about what the listener expects to hear again.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a falling-fifth sequence is built.
questions.stem: Story point SP-44 asks the team to explain how a falling-fifth sequence is built and why composers reach for it so often.

answer.exemplar: A falling-fifth sequence takes a short motif and restates it a perfect fifth lower each time, so the figure appears to be carried down through the key. Because the fifth is the most stable interval, the repetitions feel firmly grounded even as they move, and because the harmony is driven by a chain of dominants the passage generates strong forward momentum. That combination of economy and energy is why the pattern is so widely used in extended writing.

questions.explanation: A falling-fifth sequence restates the motif a fifth lower each time. It builds long passages from little material and gives the music a strong sense of onward motion.
questions.hint: Ask what interval separates one statement from the next.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a texture fugal rather than merely polyphonic.
questions.stem: Compliance ask CA-9 asks the team to explain what a fugal texture has that a freely polyphonic passage does not.

answer.exemplar: A fugal texture is generated by imitation: one voice states the subject, another states the answer to it, and further voices do the same in turn, so the whole texture grows out of one melodic idea. Freely polyphonic writing can have just as many independent lines, but nothing about them is derived from a shared subject, and the lines are written to sound well together rather than to follow one another. The subject and its answer are therefore what separate a fugal texture from polyphony in general.

questions.explanation: A fugal texture is generated by imitation, with each voice entering in turn with the subject and its answer. Freely polyphonic writing may have several independent lines without any shared subject.
questions.hint: Look for the imitation between the voices.

options.text: Minor second, minor third, whole tone, then perfect fifth.
Perfect fifth, whole tone, minor third, then minor second.
options.misconception: Lists the intervals from largest down to smallest.

options.text: Minor second, whole tone, minor third, then perfect fifth.
options.misconception: Puts the whole tone ahead of the minor third.

options.misconception: Swaps the first two intervals in the list.

questions.explanation: The four intervals measure one, three, two and seven semitones, and only the whole tone and the minor third need care because two is smaller than three. Sorting by semitone count therefore gives the minor second first and the perfect fifth last.

questions.explanation: A appears three times and every other label once, so the helper returns A. That recurring label is the refrain, and the sections that appear once are the episodes between the returns.

The figure 3, because it is the only tuplet that fits a simple beat.

options.misconception: Reads the span of the compound beat as four eighths.

options.misconception: Confuses the compound quintuplet with a beat of three.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a hemiola is written and what the player is asked to do.
questions.stem: Docs ticket DT-9 asks the team to explain how a hemiola is written in 6/8 and what the player is actually asked to do.

answer.exemplar: In 6/8 a hemiola keeps the same six eighth notes but regroups them as three beats of two eighths instead of the meter's two beats of three. The notation shows this by beaming the six notes in pairs, often with a numeral three over the pair groups, so the player holds the same total duration but articulates three even beats. Because the accents now fall at the third and fifth eighth notes, the bar contradicts the compound metre it is written in.

questions.explanation: The hemiola is written as two groups of three eighth notes with a beam or figure that shows three against the metrical two. The player simply holds the six eighths but feels them as three even beats.
questions.hint: Same six notes, a different way of feeling them.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a falling-fifth sequence from a list of motives.
questions.stem: Audit finding AF-12 lists four motives: B falling to F then to C, a line dropping by whole tones, a line dropping by semitones, and a line rising by thirds. Which one is the falling-fifth sequence?

options.text: The motive that steps down a fifth each time, such as B, F, C, G.
The motive that steps down a whole tone each time, such as C, Bb, Ab.
options.misconception: Confuses a whole-tone sequence with a falling-fifth sequence.

options.text: The motive that steps down a semitone each time, such as C, B, Bb.
options.misconception: Reads a chromatic descent as the diatonic fifth pattern.

options.text: The motive that leaps up a third each time, such as C, E, G, Bb.
options.misconception: Takes rising major thirds as the classic sequence.

questions.explanation: A falling-fifth sequence transposes the motive down a perfect fifth, so B is followed by F and then by C. Whole-tone and chromatic descents are also sequences, but they use different transposing intervals.

options.misconception: Swaps the two episodes in the ranking.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Contrast binary and ternary form in their use of repetition.
questions.stem: Rollout ticket RO-2 asks the team to explain how binary and ternary form differ in their use of repetition, not just in their number of sections.

answer.exemplar: In binary form the two large sections are normally both new, so the second section answers the first by contrast and the movement ends where the plan says it ends. In ternary form the middle section is the contrasting one and the outer sections are the same material, so the repetition is structural: the opening returns after the journey away. That is why a ternary movement sounds rounded and a binary one sounds linear.

questions.explanation: Binary form usually presents two new sections with no large-scale return. Ternary form builds on a repeat, returning the first section after the contrasting middle, so the form closes on material the listener knows.
questions.hint: Ask whether the opening comes back at the end.

questions.stem: A canon chart records a leader entering on G, a follower on D and a second follower on C. How does the second follower relate to the leader?

The second follower is a fifth below the leader, since D is a fifth above G.

options.misconception: Assumes a shared source means a common pitch.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sequence creates forward motion in a passage.
questions.stem: Story point SP-58 asks the team to explain why a sequence gives a passage a sense of forward motion.

answer.exemplar: A sequence creates forward motion because the listener can predict what is coming. The motif is stated clearly the first time, so from then on the ear is waiting for it to return at the same distance, and each repetition confirms that expectation while carrying the music further. Because the interval of transposition is regular, the movement sounds driven rather than accidental, and because the figure is being reshaped at each step the passage also continues to develop rather than simply looping.

questions.explanation: A sequence keeps the same shape but moves it, so the ear hears the pattern continuing without the music ever resting. The regularity of the interval makes the motion feel purposeful rather than arbitrary.
questions.hint: Think about what the ear follows from one repeat to the next.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the three textures of the course are distinguished.
questions.stem: Training request TR-45 asks the team to explain how the three textures the course covers are told apart in a score.

answer.exemplar: Monophonic texture carries one melodic line with nothing sounding against it, and the test is whether any second part could be removed. Two-part texture splits the music between two lines that move in counterpoint, so it is already polyphonic but needs only two voices. Fugal texture adds further voices on top, and the essential test there is imitation: each voice enters in turn with the subject and then its answer, so the texture is generated by the imitation rather than by accompaniment.

questions.explanation: Monophony has a single line, two-part writing divides the music between two lines, and fugal writing layers several voices that each present the subject and its answer. Each step adds independent lines rather than just more notes.
questions.hint: Count the independent lines and check for imitation.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a hemiola does to the accent pattern of a compound bar.
questions.stem: Support request SR-29 asks the team to explain what happens to the accent pattern of a 6/8 bar when a hemiola is applied.

answer.exemplar: In 6/8 the two compound beats are marked by the first and the fourth eighth notes, so the bar divides into two groups of three. A hemiola regroups the same six notes as three pairs, and the accents move to the first, third and fifth eighth notes. Nothing about the pitch or the length of the notes changes; only the way they are weighted and grouped does, and that is enough to make the listener hear three beats inside a bar that notates two.

questions.explanation: A hemiola moves the accents of a 6/8 bar from the first and fourth eighth notes to the first, third and fifth, so the bar is felt in three beats rather than two. The notes are unchanged, only their weight and grouping.
questions.hint: Compare where the strong notes fall in each grouping.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Count the independent voices in a mixed texture.
questions.stem: Support request SR-71 describes a passage with a melody, an independent counter-line and a chordal accompaniment. How many independent voices does the passage contain?
questions.explanation: Only the melody and the counter-line are independent, so the passage has two independent voices. The chordal accompaniment supports the melody and would not stand on its own, so it is not counted.
questions.hint: Count only the lines that would make sense alone.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.learningObjective: Order four texture descriptions from simplest to most complex.
questions.stem: Review note RN-95 asks which option orders four texture descriptions from the simplest to the most complex.

options.text: A single unaccompanied line, a tune over chords, two moving lines, four imitating lines.
A tune over chords, a single unaccompanied line, two moving lines, four imitating lines.
options.misconception: Swaps the first two descriptions in the order.

options.text: A single unaccompanied line, two moving lines, a tune over chords, four imitating lines.
options.misconception: Moves the chordal texture ahead of the two-part one.

options.text: Two moving lines, four imitating lines, a single unaccompanied line, a tune over chords.
options.misconception: Starts the list with the most complex texture.

questions.explanation: One bare line is the starting point, a tune with chords adds a layer that still supports it, two moving lines give real counterpoint, and four imitating lines build the fullest texture of the four. The order therefore follows the amount of independent material.
questions.hint: Look at how many lines move on their own in each.
